newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-EMU hopeful Portugal sees rosy start to 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMU hopeful Portugal sees rosy start to 1997.

text.p: Portugual, seeking to make the grade for a single European currency, said on Wednesday it had indications of a better economic performance in the early part of 1997 than it had anticipated.
Portuguese Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco, in London to discuss plans for Portugal's largest privatisation ever, said inflation and deficit data so far exceeded expectations.
In an interview with Reuters, Franco also said the sale of state electricity company EDP-Electricidade de Portugal would probably involve a "golden share" for the government.

European governments are working hard to meet a three percent public deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) requirement as laid out in the Maastricht Treaty for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Portugal has forecast a 2.9 percent deficit/GDP ratio in 1997.
"We only have results of the first three months. The results are very good from an expenditure and a receipts side," Franco said. "We had targets for those months and they have been exceeded."
He said Portugal collected more receipts than expected and spending was held to levels predicted.
"I don't see a need for any additional discretionary measures to achieve the 2.9 percent but should they be necessary of course they would be approved."
On the inflation front Franco said March data so far also looked better than expected.
"We have first estimates of inflation concerning March -- very provisional...but they are better than we had foreseen," he said.
Asked if he was worried about robust growth this year leading to inflationary pressures, Franco said, "I don't see any factors that would have a strong inflationary impact."

In February, Portugal recorded a 2.9 percent year-on-year rate of inflatioon, or 3.2 percent on the rolling 12-month average. When the data were released, in mid-March, analysts said they meant the government's goal of bringing the average figure down to 2.25-to-2.50 percent was possible.
Franco said on Wednesday 2.50 percent would be "reasonable".
He also said the level of long-term Portuguese interest rates, relative to benchmark German rates, in January had indicated market confidence that Portugal would be in the first wave of EMU members.
The euro currency is due to be introduced under EMU on January 1, 1999.
Since then, the gap between Portuguese and German long-term rates had widened but the trend, Franco said, was for them to converge.
Meanwhile the privatisation of EDP, which has been valued by government consultants at up to 1.7 trillion escudos, is set to become the largest privatisation ever carried out in Portugal.
Franco said it would probably be necessary to have a golden share in EDP.
A golden share is generally a stake in a company which allows the holder to maintain a degree of power, typically achieved by allowing sufficient voting rights.
Last week Portugal's State Secretary for Industry and Energy Jose Penedos said the sale could slip from mid-May to June in order to avoid a clash with the planned float of France Telecom.
Franco said the "base" amount of the privatisation was 25 percent and the total would be much less than the maxium amount allowed, which was 49 percent.
